title: Parameters, Arguments, and Return Values
learningObjectives: Explain the key vocabulary and behavior covered in this topic.
Distinguish related concepts using a small program example.
Trace how information or execution moves through the example.
Identify a common mistake and explain its consequence.
Apply the concept in a new programming scenario.

understand.concept: Parameters are named input slots in a function definition. Arguments are the concrete values or expressions supplied at a call. A return value is the result a function sends back to its caller; printing is a separate action and does not itself return a value. Functions may accept zero, one, or many inputs, and some languages support defaults or named arguments.
understand.whyItMatters: Clear input/output boundaries make functions adaptable and easier to test. Confusing printed output with a return value often breaks calculations that need to reuse results.
understand.analogy: Think of a function as a service counter: parameters describe what it can accept, arguments are the items you hand over, and the return value is what it gives back. The analogy does not cover every language's calling rules.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy simplifies language-specific rules; verify the actual language semantics when applying the idea.

explain.narrative: Read a function signature as a description of the information it expects. At a call site, arguments are matched to parameters according to the language. A returned value can be stored, passed to another function, or used in an expression. If a function only prints, the caller may have no usable result.

examples.title: Two parameters
examples.code:
function total(price, count) { return price * count; }
console.log(total(8, 3));
examples.explanation: The two arguments fill two parameter positions in order.

examples.explanation: The caller stores the function's returned value in sum.

examples.title: Use returned value in another call
examples.explanation: The return from square becomes an argument to plusOne.

commonMistakes: Confusing a definition with its execution.
Assuming all languages share the same syntax or scope rules.
Ignoring the difference between visible output and returned data.
Using unclear names or undocumented assumptions.
Skipping checks for unusual or invalid inputs.

guidedTask.title: Guided practice: parameters, arguments, and return values
guidedTask.instructions: Create a small example demonstrating parameters, arguments, and return values. Predict behavior before running, then explain the concept in your own words.
steps: Write a small function focused on one behavior.
Label or document the key concept being demonstrated.
Test at least two cases, including an edge case where relevant.
Explain how the concept affects readability or reliability.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Start with one focused function and test two cases.

independentTask.title: Independent practice: apply the concept
independentTask.instructions: Build a small scenario-based program that uses this concept deliberately.
requirements: Use clear names and a single focused responsibility where possible.
Include at least two test scenarios.
Show the result and explain it.
Review for unnecessary complexity or hidden side effects.

hints: Write the smallest useful example first.
Trace each input and output carefully.
Test a normal and boundary case.
Use the concept to improve clarity, not to add complexity.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the central concept in this lesson?
options: A clearly defined function behavior or boundary
A guarantee that every language works identically
questions.answer: A clearly defined function behavior or boundary
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes understanding behavior and boundaries rather than assuming universal syntax.

questions.prompt: Why should programmers make assumptions explicit?
options: It helps callers use code correctly and tests verify expectations
It makes code run without inputs
questions.answer: It helps callers use code correctly and tests verify expectations
questions.explanation: Explicit assumptions and checks make behavior easier to review and test.

questions.prompt: What is a good first step when tracing the example?
options: Identify the inputs and follow execution in order
Guess the output and skip the code
questions.answer: Identify the inputs and follow execution in order
questions.explanation: A careful trace follows values and statements step by step.

options: Use clear names and focused responsibilities
Copy the same logic into unrelated locations
questions.answer: Use clear names and focused responsibilities
questions.explanation: Clear naming and focus help readers understand and safely modify code.

questions.prompt: What should a learner do after an initial test succeeds?
options: Try additional cases, including boundaries when appropriate
questions.answer: Try additional cases, including boundaries when appropriate
questions.explanation: More cases can reveal assumptions or behavior that a single test misses.
